content.thinking:
I need to write the postmortem using placeholder names rather than inventing figures. There's a discrepancy to note carefully: the flag changes are logged as recorded at 20:06:45Z, but the evaluation logs show the actual flip happening at 20:01 — I should surface this timing gap rather than gloss over it.

The root cause points to the legacy-checkout-fallback flag being turned off, which routed account pages to the new renderer; that renderer computes average spend per item by dividing by the length of the purchase list, which crashes for shoppers with no purchases this month. The monthly-spend-feature revert didn't fix things, ruling that flag out as the cause. Since the code-level explanation rests only on an unverified reading from the F rows, I need to flag that this step in the causal chain is unverified, while still treating the chain as reaching a cause since the crash itself is confirmed by the log evidence.

I should avoid citing exact failure counts since there's a mismatch between the reported 49 and the log's 11 occurrences, and I'll note the baseline ClientDisconnected noise as unrelated. For impact and detection, I need to describe the error rate rise, duration, and alert timing using the placeholder values, and note that the response was slowed because the first mitigation attempt picked the wrong flag to revert.

Two flags changed in the same minute by the same admin, making it impossible to isolate which one caused the regression, and the thread lead's correct hypothesis was initially dismissed as unverified, costing time before the right flag was reverted. For action items, I'm thinking the process should require testing flag changes one at a time or in parallel with clear attribution when multiple flags move together, and that renderer-path toggles need canary rollouts since disabling the legacy fallback routed traffic into a path with an unfixed bug — this calls for staged rollout guards rather than instant flips.

I also noticed the change-event feed missed the flag toggles entirely, since they came from the flag provider's own history rather than the monitored changes source; fixing this means pulling flag provider history into the initial change read. On the investigation side, correlating renderer-routing counts with flag evaluation counts before choosing which flag to revert would have sped things up, matching what eventually happened once counts were checked — though the thread lead's hypothesis didn't actually change the order of actions taken, it just matched where things ended up.

Now I'm laying out the causal chain with citations: the user-facing account page failures traced to a ZeroDivisionError in the new renderer, which was active because the legacy-checkout-fallback flag flipped off at 20:01, routing roughly a quarter of evaluations through the broken path. The monthly-spend-feature flag also changed around the same time but was ruled out since reverting it didn't help and there were no deploys to explain the coincidence.

Drilling further, I believe the renderer likely divides by the count of this month's purchases without guarding against an empty list, causing the crash -- though this read is from static analysis and not fully verified. I'm noting that I can't confirm why that code path was left unguarded, so I'll state the root cause with that caveat rather than asserting certainty.

I also want to avoid writing specific timestamps or line numbers in the final text, using phrasing like "at the onset" instead, and confirm the mitigation restored error rates to normal.

action_items.item: Add a regression test, and a check in the release path, that renders the account page for a shopper with past purchases but none this month, through both the legacy and new renderers, so it fails before a flag can route traffic to it.
Require a staged rollout or a review for toggling flags that choose the renderer for account pages. Also require changes to flags that affect the same page to be made one at a time, not together.

Make the investigation read the flag provider's change history at the start, alongside the production change events. When several flags changed together, compare each flag's evaluation counts with the failing path's counts before choosing which one to revert first.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw failed account pages: the error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average, peaking at {errors_at_worst}, for {duration}, and the HighErrorRate alert fired.
The failing requests raised ZeroDivisionError in spend_summary.py, and account pages were being served by the new renderer instead of the legacy one.

The new renderer was serving them because legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off at the onset. Before that it evaluated on for every evaluation, and at the onset a share of evaluations turned off. monthly-spend-feature was switched on in the same minute, but reverting it did not improve the service, so it was ruled out. No deploy or other production change was recorded.
Reverting legacy-checkout-fallback to on brought the service back below the incident's level, which confirms that this flag routed traffic to the failing path.

The new renderer fails because the monthly average-spend calculation divides by the count of this month's purchases, which is empty for a shopper who bought before but not this month. This rests on Code-Fix's static reading of the source, which is unverified because nothing ran it.

contributing_factors.factor: The calculation in the new renderer was left unguarded against an empty monthly purchase list, and no test or check that covered this case was seen. A flag change could therefore send ordinary traffic into it.
An admin switched two flags in the same minute, so the cause could not be told apart from the logs alone. No staged rollout or guard on the flag change was seen.

The first mitigation reverted monthly-spend-feature, the wrong flag, and cost a wait before it was judged refuted. The thread lead naming the correct flag was set aside as unverified, and the production-change read returned nothing even though the flag provider's history showed both toggles.

input.executive_summary: For {duration}, from {began}, a share of account-page requests on io-shop failed. The error rate went from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average and peaked at {errors_at_worst}, so about {errors_rise} of traffic failed that otherwise would not have. Shoppers who opened their account page got an error instead. Two feature flags had been switched in the same minute. Argus first reverted the wrong one, which did not help. It then reverted the other flag, legacy-checkout-fallback, and the error rate returned to normal by {back_to_normal}. A draft pull request fixing the underlying calculation has been proposed and is awaiting review.

lead_effects.effect: It did not change the first action, which reverted monthly-spend-feature and was refuted, but the second action reverted legacy-checkout-fallback as the lead said and was confirmed.

got_lucky: Both flags were easy to revert, so testing one and then the other cost only a wait. Had the second flag not been the cause, the record shows no further fallback.
went_well: Argus detected the fault, read the flag history, and acted within seconds of forming candidates.
The refuted action was judged and put back, so the wrong flag was not left changed.
The second candidate was backed by matching counts, and its revert was confirmed against the metrics, after which the paging rule stopped firing.
A draft fix was proposed right after mitigation.
went_wrong: The first revert targeted monthly-spend-feature, which was not the cause, so the service stayed broken longer than needed.
The thread lead that pointed at the correct flag was weighed as unverified and did not change the first action.
The production change read returned nothing, although two flag toggles were in the flag provider's history.

input.root_cause: The legacy-checkout-fallback flag was switched off, which sent account pages to the new renderer. In that renderer the monthly average-spend calculation divides by the number of this month's purchases. From a static reading of the code (unverified, nothing ran it), that list is empty for a shopper who has bought before but not this month, so the page raises ZeroDivisionError and is served as a failure. The record does not show why this code path was never exercised before the flag was switched off.
